title: Photo Backup Sentinel
user: iPhone and Android owners who copy photos to an external drive or NAS and need to know, before storage fills or a phone is lost, that every new photo and Live Photo has a second usable copy.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The poster describes the common storage problem: iPhone storage fills quickly, iCloud subscriptions are unwanted, and a NAS is unrealistic for many people.
A 25-reaction request asks for background iOS photo backup with Wi-Fi/charging controls and repeated-failure notifications.

recurrence: Two independent backup communities identify the same failure mode: copying is not proof of backup. The loss risk is severe and recurs whenever mobile background transfer is interrupted.
current_workaround: Trust the camera roll, periodically drag folders to a drive, pay for cloud storage, or operate a full NAS/photo server.
incumbents_and_gap: iCloud Photos, Google Photos, iMazing, and Immich move or sync photos. They do not give a lightweight, device-agnostic proof that recent media—including paired motion assets—exists on two readable destinations.
smallest_useful_product: A desktop-local app that scans a phone export and one backup destination, matches media by content/metadata, highlights unprotected recent items, and runs a sampled open/read verification. Non-goals: cloud hosting, photo editing, or a replacement photo library.
success_measure: In a 30-day pilot, 70% of users run at least three checks and 25% discover and repair one missing or unreadable asset.
monetization: one-time — backup verification is a trust utility whose value should not require keeping media on a vendor server.
constraints: Process media locally; preserve but do not upload EXIF/location data; clearly distinguish a hash match from a playback verification; iOS access is limited to user-provided exports/files.
why_distinct: It verifies backup completeness and restoreability instead of offering another photo-sync destination.

title: Photo Exit Bundle
user: Families leaving or reducing reliance on Google Photos who need a usable local photo archive without losing albums, dates, motion companions, or a simple way to share with mixed-device relatives.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A Pixel-owning parent has outgrown Google storage, worries about account lockout, and explicitly wishes for an easy way to back up Google Photos.
The request notes that Google Photos and Drive behavior differ and that a 300k-photo collection makes manual migration impractical (37 reactions, 171 comments).

recurrence: Account-lockout anxiety, growing family libraries, and storage bills turn this into a recurring exit problem; the rclone thread's long discussion shows the integration is persistently awkward.
current_workaround: Download Takeout ZIPs, use rclone scripts, switch to another cloud, or self-host Immich/PhotoPrism and manually repair metadata.
incumbents_and_gap: Google Takeout exports data and rclone copies files; Immich and PhotoPrism host libraries. The missing middle is a local, explainable migration report that identifies what survived and what needs user attention.
smallest_useful_product: A local Takeout-to-folder converter that pairs JSON metadata and motion-video files, recreates dated folders/album manifests, produces a duplicate and missing-companion report, and writes a portable README. Non-goals: Google API scraping, hosted galleries, or face recognition.
success_measure: At least 80% of pilot exports finish with fewer than 1% unclassified assets and users open the resulting archive on a second machine.
monetization: one-time — it is a finite migration with no credible reason to retain family photos.
constraints: Runs entirely on user-selected files; do not claim full fidelity for unsupported Google metadata; preserve originals; comply with Google Takeout formats and avoid account automation.
why_distinct: This is an exit-quality checker and portable archive builder, not a Google Photos clone or another sync daemon.

title: Archive Restore Rehearsal
user: People with years of files across many USB disks who need a practical archive map and evidence that a random sample can still be restored and opened.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A 1.7 TB backup user says CrashPlan costs $30/month, finds the interface clunky, and rejects sync-only cloud storage because accidental deletion is not a real backup.
A 369-reaction, 99-comment backup issue asks for a different recovery topology: a dedicated machine pulling data from systems rather than only pushing backups outward.

recurrence: Personal archives grow gradually until hardware, file-system, and location diversity makes an untested backup indistinguishable from no backup; the cost of discovery is loss.
current_workaround: Label drives informally, use RAID or a backup CLI, create a spreadsheet, and only attempt restoration after a disk fails.
incumbents_and_gap: restic, Backblaze, and NAS products make copies; disk cataloguers list files. Few consumer-oriented tools turn disparate copies into a restore drill with a clear archive ownership map.
smallest_useful_product: A local app that inventories mounted drives, records content hashes and physical labels, proposes a small rotating restore sample, opens supported files to prove readability, and exports a printable recovery card. Non-goals: copying data, cloud backup, or RAID management.
success_measure: 50% of activated users complete a first restore drill within 14 days, and at least 20% correct a mislabeled, missing, or unreadable archive copy.
monetization: one-time — archive owners need durable local reporting, not another storage subscription.
constraints: Never modify source media by default; handle huge directories incrementally; hashes and local path names may be sensitive; clearly mark removable-drive identity as fallible.
why_distinct: It measures recoverability, not backup throughput or storage capacity.

title: PDF Flow Reader
user: Knowledge workers with low vision who need long PDFs to read as stable, keyboard-first reflowed prose rather than zoomed page images or broken screen-reader line fragments.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A knowledge worker gradually losing vision asks how to adapt across Office, Teams, Google Docs, Confluence, Salesforce, and PowerBI; commenters cite expensive or platform-limited readers.
A 2025 PDF.js accessibility report says VoiceOver reads each line of a paragraph independently while macOS Preview recognizes the paragraph correctly.

recurrence: Low-vision workers need reliable reading tools daily, and even a mature open PDF viewer still has document-structure failures that make long reading exhausting.
current_workaround: Increase browser zoom, use OS magnification/inverted contrast, buy a screen reader, or switch between viewers until one happens to expose usable text.
incumbents_and_gap: VoiceOver, NVDA, Acrobat, and PDF.js cover broad accessibility needs. The gap is a focused local reader that makes a chosen PDF's extracted reading flow visibly inspectable and quickly adjustable without pretending to repair the original document.
smallest_useful_product: A browser-based local PDF reader with a single-column reflow mode, adjustable line/word spacing and contrast, heading navigation, keyboard reading position, and an explicit extraction-confidence warning. Non-goals: legal accessibility certification, PDF editing, or cloud OCR.
success_measure: In moderated sessions, 8 of 10 low-vision users can resume a saved reading position and complete a 10-minute reading task with fewer viewer switches than their normal workflow.
monetization: free — accessibility benefit and local trust outweigh paywall complexity; optional paid support can follow.
constraints: Keep documents on-device; respect encrypted/permission-protected PDFs; do not claim text extraction fixes a source document's WCAG compliance; maintain keyboard and screen-reader accessibility of the tool itself.
why_distinct: It is a personal reading adaptation layer, not a generic PDF editor or automated compliance checker.

title: Scan to Study Pack
user: Students and independent readers with legitimately obtained scanned PDFs who need searchable, citeable text and page links without sending the document to a cloud AI service.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The asker repeatedly screenshots pages into ChatGPT because scanned philosophy PDFs are hard to read/search; the 57-comment thread recommends a mixture of command-line and cloud OCR tools.
A 2025 issue reports a local OCR workflow failing at the Tesseract step, illustrating that self-hosted OCR remains brittle for non-specialists.

recurrence: Scanned readings are common in education and archives; the current route is either repetitive page-by-page cloud work or a technical OCR installation.
current_workaround: Use pdftotext when lucky, run Tesseract/Docker, manually screenshot pages into an LLM, or accept an unsearchable scan.
incumbents_and_gap: Adobe Acrobat and cloud OCR services are capable; Tesseract/Stirling are powerful but configuration-heavy. There is room for an offline, failure-transparent study artifact rather than a full document-management suite.
smallest_useful_product: A local PWA that runs OCR on user-selected pages, shows side-by-side page/text alignment, flags low-confidence blocks, and exports Markdown/HTML with page anchors and citation snippets. Non-goals: hosting books, bulk piracy workflows, or AI summaries.
success_measure: 60% of pilot users export a study pack from a 50-page scan, with at least 90% of sampled quotations traceable back to the correct page.
monetization: one-time — offline document conversion has clear per-user value and should not require retaining reading material.
constraints: Only process user-provided material; no library/distribution feature; WASM OCR performance and language packs must be disclosed; preserve source-page attribution and copyright notices.
why_distinct: The output is a verifiable study pack with page provenance, not a thin OCR/LLM upload front end.

title: Personal Data Exit Map
user: People leaving a service or preparing for lockout who need a sober inventory of their export, what can be reused elsewhere, and what account-dependent data will remain behind.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Ask HN poster explicitly asks why there is no comprehensive open-source way to export, import, or transfer personal data across online services.
A 631-reaction migration issue explains that moving followers is only a small part of a real exit: users also want their posts and history.

recurrence: Portability pain appears whenever a service shuts down, locks an account, changes terms, or raises prices; even federated products leave meaningful history behind.
current_workaround: Download opaque export ZIPs, keep an untested drive copy, follow scattered migration guides, or give up on preserving useful metadata.
incumbents_and_gap: Takeout and individual service exports move bytes; migration services target a few platforms. The missing product is a local exit assessment that tells a non-expert what an export contains and gives them durable next actions.
smallest_useful_product: A local web app that opens supported export archives, creates a file/metadata inventory, detects common reusable formats, produces a preservation checklist and a signed manifest, and links to manual export steps for unsupported services. Non-goals: credential collection, scraping, API circumvention, or universal import claims.
success_measure: 75% of test users can answer where their top five data categories are stored and complete one verified export within a single session.
monetization: free — trust and broad compatibility improve through community parsers; paid guided migration can be considered later.
constraints: Never ask for account passwords or upload exports; parser plugins must be sandboxed; label formats/version support precisely; do not imply an export preserves legal access rights or social relationships.
why_distinct: It is an exit-readiness and preservation utility, not another cloud-to-cloud transfer service.

title: Tab Context Capsule
user: Researchers and knowledge workers with overloaded browser sessions who need to stop, hand off, and resume a small project context without trusting a browser's fragile tab restore.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A current Ask HN asks how people handle browser-tab overload; one response recommends closing most tabs, underscoring that context is discarded rather than captured.
A 44-comment Firefox iOS regression reports an update deleting every open tab, including inactive and private ones.

recurrence: Tab accumulation is routine, while browser updates, crashes, and device changes make open-tab state an unreliable project record.
current_workaround: Leave tabs open, create bookmark folders, use OneTab/session managers, or paste a rough list into notes before closing a window.
incumbents_and_gap: Browser tab groups, OneTab, and sync preserve URLs. They rarely preserve a concise human explanation of why each page mattered, the next action, and a portable handoff bundle.
smallest_useful_product: A browser extension that turns selected tabs into a named capsule with title, URL, optional one-line note, ordering, next step, and Markdown/JSON export; it can reopen a capsule locally. Non-goals: cloud sync, browsing-history analytics, or LLM summarization.
success_measure: At least 50% of active users create two capsules in their first week and reopen or share one after closing the original tabs.
monetization: one-time — the core asset is a local portable file, not a collaboration SaaS.
constraints: Request minimal tab permissions; private-window support must be opt-in and never silently persisted; never transmit browsing URLs; exports may contain sensitive links.
why_distinct: It converts fragile tab state into a deliberate, explainable project handoff rather than another tab hoarder.

title: Family Digital Dossier
user: Adults who want a trusted family member or executor to locate essential digital records during illness or death without handing over their entire password vault today.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The asker worries that family would not know how to find banking, investments, wills, insurance, or documents; a commenter keeps an encrypted repository inventory in a separate secure location.
The emergency-access request describes a timeout-based trusted-contact flow for medical accidents or death and asks to limit access to selected sites.

recurrence: The need is triggered by life events but preparation is repeatedly deferred because existing password tools make it all-or-nothing and paperwork becomes stale.
current_workaround: Leave a paper notebook, share a master-password hint, maintain a private encrypted text file, or rely on a password manager's emergency feature alone.
incumbents_and_gap: Bitwarden, 1Password, and lawyers' estate plans address credentials or legal documents separately. The gap is a regularly reviewed locator dossier that records what exists and who to contact without storing secret credentials.
smallest_useful_product: An offline encrypted template that records institutions, document locations, renewal dates, emergency contacts, and executor instructions; it generates a review checklist and a printable sealed-cover sheet. Non-goals: password storage, legal advice, will generation, or automated account access.
success_measure: 60% of users complete at least ten locator entries and perform a scheduled six-month review; test recipients can locate three requested records using only the generated dossier.
monetization: one-time — a local continuity document should remain usable without a recurring account or vendor survival risk.
constraints: Client-side encryption with a clearly explained recovery model; collect no credentials by design; present jurisdiction-specific legal limitations prominently; users control print/storage security.
why_distinct: It fills the practical inventory-and-handoff gap around password managers instead of competing as one.

title: Feed Later Bridge
user: RSS readers who mark articles for later but do not want a separate proprietary read-later silo or a manual copy/paste routine.

evidence.quote_or_summary: An Instapaper user wants read-later items to arrive in their RSS reader workflow rather than maintaining two platforms.
A 32-reaction request asks Wallabag to regularly import an RSS feed of articles marked for later in another reader.

recurrence: Read-later and RSS workflows keep splitting even for people who intentionally use feeds; the same desired bridge appears in independent communities.
current_workaround: Use Instapaper/Pocket plus a reader, manually save links again, depend on a service-specific integration, or abandon one workflow.
incumbents_and_gap: Wallabag, Raindrop, and RSS readers have partial integrations. A tiny local bridge that treats RSS/Atom as a transparent handoff format and keeps an exportable queue is still uncommon.
smallest_useful_product: A local-first web/extension pair that imports a user-designated RSS/Atom saved-items feed, deduplicates entries, lets the user mark/annotate a compact queue, and exports OPML/Markdown/JSON. Non-goals: article scraping at scale, social feeds, recommendations, or hosted accounts.
success_measure: 50% of pilots import a feed and export or finish at least ten saved items in 30 days without creating a vendor account.
monetization: free — open feed interoperability and local files are central to the value; paid sync would be optional later.
constraints: Fetch feeds only from user-provided URLs; protect against feed HTML/script injection and SSRF in any companion service; retain only local reading metadata by default.
why_distinct: It is a standards-based handoff bridge, not a new reader or attention-maximizing content feed.

title: Reading Archive Pack
user: People displaced by Pocket-style shutdowns who need to turn a read-later export into a durable, searchable Markdown archive rather than choose another fragile subscription.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The asker says many read-it-later products are dead or abandoned after Pocket's shutdown; commenters fall back to self-hosting or saving standalone HTML files.
Wallabag users requested Markdown export because it is editable, lightweight, and compatible with many applications (12 reactions).

recurrence: Service shutdowns repeatedly strand reading queues and annotations; users explicitly value a format they can edit with ordinary tools.
current_workaround: Move to another hosted reader, self-host Wallabag, keep an export ZIP unused, or save pages manually as HTML/PDF.
incumbents_and_gap: Instapaper, Wallabag, Raindrop, and Readwise keep libraries inside their own models. Export options exist unevenly, but users lack a simple migration verifier that creates a clean archival folder with link-health accounting.
smallest_useful_product: A local converter for Pocket/Instapaper/Wallabag exports that creates one Markdown file per item with metadata and annotations, optionally attaches user-downloaded HTML, and emits a report of inaccessible or duplicate URLs. Non-goals: a new read-later service, content crawling, or AI summaries.
success_measure: 80% of pilot imports produce a usable Markdown folder and at least 50% of users open it in a second notes/file application within one week.
monetization: one-time — this is a finite migration and the output must outlive the product.
constraints: Only process user exports and pages they choose to save; respect site terms and copyright; make failed fetches visible; sanitize saved HTML and avoid storing credentials.
why_distinct: It is a durable exit package with verification, not another bookmark database.

title: CSV Import Cleanroom
user: Operations staff and solo administrators preparing a messy spreadsheet for a strict SaaS import template who need a repeatable, auditable conversion without writing Python or damaging the original file.

evidence.quote_or_summary: People importing into Salesforce, Workday, and NetSuite describe recurring date, schema, and template-alignment cleanup; replies point to Excel or custom scripts.
A 334-reaction request shows how even personal imports become difficult when categories and transactions have different currencies and normalization rules.

recurrence: Template imports recur in onboarding, migration, and periodic operations, and small inconsistencies become costly rejected rows or silent bad records.
current_workaround: Edit the only copy in Excel, use brittle formulas, ask an engineer for a script, or repeatedly upload trial files until an importer accepts them.
incumbents_and_gap: Excel/Google Sheets, OpenRefine, and ETL tools can transform rows. The gap is a friendly offline preflight that saves the exact mapping recipe and explains import failures in the target template's language.
smallest_useful_product: A local CSV tool with side-by-side source/target columns, named transforms for dates/currency/IDs, validation rules, rejected-row explanations, and a reusable JSON recipe. Non-goals: direct SaaS credentials, database ETL, automatic data inference, or LLM transformations.
success_measure: At least 70% of test users produce an accepted target CSV on the first import attempt after using a saved recipe.
monetization: one-time — sensitive operational spreadsheets should be cleanable without a continuing upload subscription.
constraints: All parsing and transformations occur locally; protect against CSV formula injection in previews/exports; show lossy transformations before applying them; input size limits must be explicit.
why_distinct: The primary artifact is a human-reviewable, repeatable import recipe—not a spreadsheet clone or broad ETL platform.

title: PDF Accessibility Preflight
user: Small organizations and independent document authors who need to catch obvious PDF reading-order, heading, table, and form-field failures before sharing a document with screen-reader users.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A developer asks how teams with zero accessibility budget can make websites and tools usable; the thread calls for practical help for everyday developers and students rather than enterprise audits.
PDF.js tracks the need to expose embedded PDF accessibility tags for headings, tables, form fields, graphics, and alternative text.

recurrence: Accessibility is frequently deferred by small teams because specialist audits are costly, while a PDF's semantic failures are invisible to its author until a user reports them.
current_workaround: Rely on a source application's export option, run an expensive enterprise checker, manually inspect tags in Acrobat, or wait for a support complaint.
incumbents_and_gap: Acrobat Pro, PAC, and enterprise accessibility platforms are capable but intimidating or workflow-heavy. The gap is a private first-pass explainer that shows non-specialists what a viewer is likely to expose, not merely a compliance score.
smallest_useful_product: A local PDF tool that inspects the tag tree and extracted reading order, previews keyboard/screen-reader navigation, flags untagged headings/tables/forms, and exports a plain-language repair checklist. Non-goals: certifying WCAG/PDF-UA compliance, editing the PDF, or replacing expert audits.
success_measure: In usability tests, 8 of 10 non-specialist authors can identify and describe three actionable document fixes after uploading a known-problem PDF.
monetization: free — low-cost preflight helps more authors make documents accessible; paid expert workflow integrations can follow only if demand appears.
constraints: Documents never leave the device; warnings must explain uncertainty and avoid legal compliance claims; the tool's own UI must be keyboard/screen-reader accessible; parse hostile PDFs defensively.
why_distinct: It translates a PDF's actual semantic structure into an author-facing repair plan rather than being another generic accessibility scan or PDF editor.
